title: The Black Death: How 12 Ships Brought the Plague to Europe
youtube_title: The Black Death: How 12 Ships Brought the Plague to Europe | Full Documentary
description:
In October 1347, sick ships from the Black Sea rowed into the harbor of Messina, in Sicily. Within four years, the Black Death had killed somewhere between a third and a half of Europe. From the siege of Caffa to the birth of quarantine, this is how it happened, and how it changed the world.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #blackdeath #medievalhistory

beats.say: In the first days of October 1347, a fleet of galleys rowed into the harbor of Messina, in Sicily.
The traditional account says there were twelve of them, Genoese ships, coming home from the east.
Their crews were sick, and many were dying.
People on the quay saw painful swellings, and men spitting blood.
Within days, the people of Messina were dying too.
The city drove the ships back out to sea.
It was already too late.
Within four years, the disease those ships carried would kill somewhere between a third and a half of everyone in Europe.
This is the story of the Black Death.
To understand those ships, we have to go east, to the Black Sea.
On the Crimean peninsula stood Caffa, a busy trading port run by merchants from Genoa.
Silk, spices, grain and slaves passed through its harbor on their way to Italy.
In the 1340s, Caffa was besieged by Jani Beg, khan of the Golden Horde, the Mongol state that ruled the steppe to the north.
The quarrel began in 1343, with a brawl between Italians and Muslims at another port, called Tana.
The fighting dragged on for years.
Then, in 1346, a new enemy appeared inside the Mongol camp.
Soldiers began to fall sick and die, in huge numbers.
It was plague.
It had been moving west for years, along the trade routes of Central Asia.
In 2022, scientists found its DNA in graves near Lake Issyk-Kul, in modern Kyrgyzstan, where tombstones from 1338 and 1339 blame a pestilence.
Now it had reached the gates of Caffa.
According to an Italian notary named Gabriele de' Mussis, the dying army did something monstrous.
They loaded their own dead into catapults, and hurled them over the city walls.

show.text: What seemed like mountains of dead were thrown into the city.

beats.say: In his words, what seemed like mountains of dead were thrown into the city.
The defenders dumped as many bodies as they could into the sea.

show.label: THE CATAPULT STORY
show.sub: De' Mussis was probably not at Caffa

beats.say: But de' Mussis was writing in Italy, and he probably never saw Caffa himself.
Historians still debate whether those corpses really spread the disease.
Plague usually passes through flea bites, and it may simply have crept into the city on its own.
It was also spreading through other Black Sea ports, so Caffa was probably just one of several doors into the Mediterranean.
What we do know is this: in 1347, Italian galleys left the Black Sea for home.
Some of them carried a passenger no one could see.
The way home ran through the Bosporus, past Constantinople, and across the Mediterranean.
Constantinople itself was struck by plague in 1347.
It was one of the greatest cities in the world, and it was only the beginning.
The disease was moving with the ships, port by port.
Imagine a sailor on one of those galleys, weeks from home.
Around him, men fall sick, one after another.
First a fever, then painful swellings, then death, often within days.
In early October 1347, according to the Franciscan chronicler Michele da Piazza, twelve Genoese galleys put in at Messina.

show.text: They brought with them a plague that they carried down to the very marrow of their bones.

beats.say: He wrote that they brought a plague they carried down to the very marrow of their bones.
Anyone who so much as spoke to them, he claimed, caught a sickness that killed them.
Michele was writing about a decade later, so his details may not be exact.
But historians agree on the core of his story: sick ships from the east reached Messina that autumn.
Soon the people of Messina were sick too.
They drove the Genoese out of the harbor.
But the ships simply carried the disease somewhere else.
One galley expelled from Italy is said to have reached Marseille, in France, by November.
Others reached Genoa around the start of 1348.
Accounts say Genoa tried to drive the infected ships away, but the sickness got ashore anyway.
Inside Messina, the city came apart.
Michele describes bodies left lying in houses, while relatives searched for anyone willing to bury them.
Terrified people fled into the fields and vineyards, and toward other Sicilian towns.
Some headed for Catania, where, one account says, they found the gates locked against them.
They took the plague with them.
By spring, it would be inside the richest cities in Europe.
So what exactly came ashore at Messina?
For more than five hundred years, nobody knew.
In 1894, during an outbreak in Hong Kong, the scientist Alexandre Yersin identified the bacterium behind plague.
Yersin had trained with Louis Pasteur, and he found the germ in the bodies of the dead.
Today it carries his name: Yersinia pestis.
In 2011, researchers rebuilt its genome from victims buried in a Black Death cemetery at East Smithfield, in London.
The killer was confirmed.
Surprisingly, the medieval strain was not very different from the plague that still exists today.
Plague took three main forms.
The bubonic form caused buboes, swollen lymph nodes in the groin, the armpit or the neck.

show.text: Some of which grew as large as a common apple, others as an egg.

beats.say: In Florence, Giovanni Boccaccio wrote that some grew as large as a common apple, others as an egg.
Without treatment, most bubonic victims died, many within a week.
The pneumonic form attacked the lungs, and could pass from person to person through coughing.
Untreated, it was almost always fatal.
The septicemic form poisoned the blood, and could kill before any swelling appeared.
For a century, the explanation was simple: rats carried infected fleas, and the fleas bit people.
But the plague sometimes moved faster than rats seemed able to carry it.
In 2018, researchers modeled outbreaks in nine European cities.
In seven of them, human fleas and body lice explained the spread better than rats.
Other scientists pushed back, and the question is not settled.
Several routes may have worked at once.
Medieval doctors knew none of this.
In 1348, the medical faculty of Paris blamed a meeting of three planets, which they said had corrupted the air.
In Avignon, Pope Clement the Sixth sat between great fires, on his doctor's advice, to purify that air.
He survived.
Most people had no fires, no doctors and nowhere to run.
And in the spring of 1348, the plague reached the heart of Italy.
In the first months of 1348, plague spread from the ports of Genoa and Pisa into Tuscany.
By March, it was in Florence.
Boccaccio watched his city collapse.
He wrote that neighbors avoided each other, and that the sick were left to die alone.

show.text: Fathers and mothers were found to abandon their own children, untended, unvisited, to their fate, as if they had been strangers.

beats.say: Even fathers and mothers, he wrote, abandoned their own children, untended and unvisited, as if they had been strangers.
Each morning, bodies lay in front of the doors, more than anyone could count.

show.label: FLORENCE, 1348
show.sub: Historians estimate about half the city died

beats.say: Historians estimate Florence lost around half its people.
South of Florence, in Siena, a shoemaker and tax collector named Agnolo di Tura was keeping a chronicle.
The dying in Siena began in May.
He wrote that victims swelled beneath the armpits and in the groin, and fell over while talking.
No one could be found to bury the dead, for money or for friendship.
Great pits were dug and filled, and then more were dug.
Then he wrote the line that still echoes, almost seven centuries later.

show.text: And I, Agnolo di Tura, called the Fat, buried my five children with my own hands.
show.who: AGNOLO DI TURA · CHRONICLE OF SIENA, 1348

beats.say: And I, Agnolo di Tura, called the Fat, buried my five children with my own hands.
So many died, he wrote, that all believed it was the end of the world.
It did not stop in Italy.
It reached Paris in 1348.
That June, ships brought it to Melcombe, on the south coast of England.
In 1349, a ship from England carried it across the North Sea to Bergen, in Norway.
In the countryside, whole villages emptied, and some were never lived in again.
In Parma, in 1349, the poet Petrarch had lost his beloved Laura and many of his closest friends.

show.text: O happy posterity, who will not experience such abysmal woe and will look upon our testimony as fable.

beats.say: He wrote: O happy posterity, who will not experience such abysmal woe, and will look upon our testimony as fable.
The wave rolled on, east into Russia, into the early 1350s.
Historians estimate the Black Death killed between 25 and 50 million people in Europe.
That is somewhere between thirty and sixty percent of the population, depending on the estimate.
Recent studies of ancient pollen suggest some regions were hit far harder than others, and a few barely at all.
But where it struck hardest, terrified people wanted someone to blame.
If God had sent the plague, some reasoned, then God must be furious.
In 1349, bands of men called flagellants marched from town to town, stripped to the waist.
They whipped their own backs bloody with weighted scourges, singing hymns as they went.
They believed their suffering might persuade God to lift the plague.
Members pledged to keep it up for thirty-three and a half days, one for each year of Christ's life.
But a darker idea was spreading, even faster than the plague.
Rumors claimed that Jews were poisoning the wells.
In September 1348, at the castle of Chillon on Lake Geneva, Jewish prisoners were tortured until they confessed to a plot.
It was a lie, and Jews were dying of plague like everyone else.
But the confessions were copied and passed from city to city.
In Strasbourg, on the fourteenth of February 1349, the city's Jews were taken to their own cemetery and burned alive.
The plague had not even reached the city yet.
One chronicler put the dead at two thousand, and the community was destroyed.
Across the Rhineland and beyond, many Jewish communities were wiped out.
In 1348, Pope Clement the Sixth ordered Christians not to harm Jews, pointing out that they were dying too.
Few listened.
In October 1349, he condemned the flagellants as well.
Meanwhile, ordinary life was unraveling.
Some people locked themselves away, and others, Boccaccio wrote, drank in the taverns day and night.
The law itself broke down, because the officials who enforced it were dead or sick.
And yet, when the dying finally slowed, the survivors woke up in a very different world.
The first thing survivors noticed was the empty land.
There were not enough hands to plow the fields or bring in the harvest.
Workers who were left demanded higher wages, and often got them.
To keep their tenants, many landlords swapped the old labor duties for cash rents.
In 1349, England ordered wages held at their old levels, and in 1351 Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers.
The laws were hated, and over time they largely failed.
Anger over them helped fuel the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
Some historians see this as the beginning of the end of serfdom in western Europe.
Europe's population did not recover its old size until the sixteenth century, and Florence not until the nineteenth.
Cities also learned to fight back.
In 1377, the port of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, made arrivals from plague areas wait thirty days in isolation.
Venice later stretched it to forty, quaranta in Italian, and that is where our word quarantine comes from.
Art turned dark, too, as skeletons began to dance across walls, leading kings and peasants alike in the Dance of Death.
One famous Dance of Death was painted in Paris, in 1424.
And the plague kept coming back, again and again, for more than three hundred years.
London's Great Plague of 1665 killed around a hundred thousand people.
Marseille suffered one of the last great outbreaks in western Europe, in 1720.

show.label: PLAGUE TODAY
show.sub: Average human cases a year in the U.S.

beats.say: It has never fully gone away, and the United States still averages about seven human cases a year.
The difference now is antibiotics, and treated early, most patients survive.
Nearly seven centuries ago, a handful of sick ships rowed into a Sicilian harbor.
Europe would never be the same.
